title: The Rise of Cloud Computing: Why Every Business Is Moving to the Cloud
excerpt: From startups to global enterprises, cloud computing has become the default way to build software. Here's what's driving the shift — and what it means for your career.

content.heading: What actually changed
content.body: Twenty years ago, running a business online meant buying physical servers, housing them somewhere, and hiring people to keep them alive. That model didn't scale — you either overbought hardware you didn't need yet, or scrambled when traffic spiked past what you'd planned for. Cloud computing flipped that equation: instead of owning infrastructure, you rent exactly the compute, storage, and networking you need, and scale it up or down in minutes instead of months.

content.heading: The players and the models
content.body: Three platforms dominate the space — AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud — each offering roughly the same building blocks: virtual servers, storage, databases, and networking, accessible through a console or code. These get delivered in a few standard models: IaaS (raw infrastructure you configure yourself), PaaS (a managed platform you deploy code onto), and SaaS (fully-built software you just use). Understanding this stack is often the first real 'aha' moment for anyone starting a cloud computing course.

content.heading: Why businesses are all-in on the cloud
content.body: The appeal isn't just cost, though paying only for what you use matters. It's speed — a team can provision a new environment in minutes instead of filing a hardware request. It's scalability — an e-commerce site can handle a festival-season traffic spike without buying servers that sit idle the other eleven months. And it's resilience — cloud providers offer redundancy and failover that would be prohibitively expensive to build in-house. For most companies today, the question isn't whether to use the cloud, but how well they use it.

content.heading: What this means for your career
content.body: Cloud skills now show up in job descriptions far outside traditional 'cloud engineer' roles — developers, data analysts, and even marketing teams increasingly touch cloud services in some form. For anyone building a technical career, foundational cloud knowledge (compute, storage, networking, security basics, and hands-on experience with at least one major provider) has become as fundamental as knowing how to use Git. It's also one of the more direct paths to a strong salary, since cloud-literate professionals remain in short supply relative to demand.

content.heading: Where to start
content.body: Start with core concepts before chasing every certification badge: what a virtual machine actually is, how storage and networking work together, and the basics of identity and access management. Then get hands-on — deploy a real, simple application to a cloud instance and see what breaks. That practical exposure, more than any single certificate, is what a Cloud Computing program like ours is built around: real deployments, not just slide decks.
